dimension: Open-source reservoir operation, optimisation and forecast-informed operations (FIRO)

confirmed_sources.name: wltaylor/Robust-FIRO
confirmed_sources.kind: GitHub repo (research code for a published paper)
confirmed_sources.what_it_provides: MPCProblem.py verified at EXACTLY 194 lines. Objective confirmed line-by-line: Sf = S0 + cp.cumsum(Qf - u, axis=1) over an (NE x NL) ensemble-by-lead array; cost = (1-w)*cp.sum(cp.pos(Sf-TOCS)) + w*cp.sum(cp.neg(Sf-TOCS)); constraints u>=0, u<=u_max, plus ramp-rate bounds applied to BOTH future steps (u[0,1:] vs u[0,:-1]) and the current step (u[0,0] vs Rt). Decision variables are literally named u_max, TOCS, ramp_rate. Also verified present: model.py (13,035 B) containing simulate_cumulative() = the Cumulative Method baseline; train_EFO.py (10,173 B) risk-threshold EFO policy search; ecrps_functions.py (4,826 B) ensemble CRPS; find_median_EFO.py; 8 figure scripts. README requirements are exactly numpy, pandas, xarray, scipy, cvxpy.
confirmed_sources.relevance: Highest-value item in the sweep and it survives adversarial checking intact. The formulation maps 1:1 onto AquaSync's existing (target level, start hour, max rate) policy search and directly closes the perfect-foresight gap - AquaSync's stated biggest weakness. Small enough (~40 lines of core cvxpy) to port rather than adopt.
confirmed_sources.content_matches_claim: yes - every structural claim checked out to the line. 194 lines confirmed by wc -l; the objective, the pos/neg split, the cumsum storage propagation, the dual ramp-rate constraints and the CLARABEL solver branch are all present as described.
confirmed_sources.caveat: Two frictions the source list omitted. (1) Line 4 is a bare, unguarded `import mosek` and run() defaults to solver='MOSEK', a COMMERCIAL solver - the module will not even import without `pip install mosek`. CLARABEL is a real supported branch but you must pass it explicitly and still satisfy the mosek import (or delete line 4). (2) Only the perfect-forecast and observed-flow data ship in the repo (perfect_forecast.nc 48.5 MB, observed_flows.csv, historical_medians.csv); the HEFS and synthetic forecast arrays must be pulled from Zenodo. Also: 1 star, last pushed 2025-03-18 - this is paper-support code, not a maintained library. Units are acre-feet at Oroville, CA.
confirmed_sources.download_hint: git clone https://github.com/wltaylor/Robust-FIRO ; forecast arrays from Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15041287 (confirmed via DataCite API as 'wltaylor/Robust-FIRO: Initial Release', 2025 - zenodo.org itself returns 403 to bots)

confirmed_sources.name: wltaylor/SSJRB-FIRO-Publishing
confirmed_sources.kind: GitHub repo (research code for a published manuscript)
confirmed_sources.what_it_provides: Multi-reservoir FIRO across 14 Sacramento-San Joaquin reservoirs. All claimed files verified present: train_firo.py (3,492 B), perfect_forecast.py (1,883 B), simulate_baseline_tocs.py (2,679 B), simulate_loocv.py (8,001 B), loocv.py (2,752 B), simulate_firo.py, model.py (14,297 B), analysis.py (45,899 B). train_firo.py IS genuinely risk-threshold policy training - source comments define the 3 parameters per reservoir as: (1) days to allow zero risk (0-10), (2) slope of risk/day allowed after that (0-0.10), (3) multiplier to change TOCS (0.8-2.0), optimised with scipy differential_evolution, 42 variables total.
confirmed_sources.relevance: The risk-threshold policy parameterisation is a cheaper alternative to full MPC and the LOOCV harness is the right way to prove a forecast-informed policy generalises - directly applicable to validating an AquaSync policy beyond the single October 2021 case study.
confirmed_sources.content_matches_claim: partly - the file inventory and the risk-threshold training claim are exactly right, but perfect_forecast.py is materially misdescribed. See caveat.
confirmed_sources.caveat: CORRECTION: perfect_forecast.py is NOT 'an explicit perfect-foresight baseline isolated so the gap can be measured'. I read all 1,883 bytes: it is a data-preparation script that builds a perfect-forecast netCDF by copying observed inflows forward into a (site, time, ensemble, lead) array, plus some matplotlib plotting. It contains no reservoir model, no simulation and no gap measurement. The foresight gap is actually measured by swapping Qf in simulate_firo.py/train_firo.py. SHIPPED BUG: train_firo.py line 82 calls DE(opt_wrapper, bounds=bounds, ...) but `bounds` is only defined inside a commented-out block at line 63 - the script raises NameError as committed (one-line fix). Forecast data (data/cnrfc14d.nc) is absent from the repo; it lives on a UC Davis Box link (verified 200).

confirmed_sources.kind: GitHub repo (research code, manuscript in review)

confirmed_sources.content_matches_claim: yes - repo description and README confirm synthetic hydrology, synthetic ensemble forecasts, skill modification and a Lake Oroville FIRO model, supporting the stated manuscript.

confirmed_sources.name: rtc-tools/rtc-tools
confirmed_sources.what_it_provides: Verified by shallow clone: src/ contains EXACTLY 16,410 lines of Python across 46 files. ControlTreeMixin confirmed at src/rtctools/optimization/control_tree_mixin.py, docstring 'Adds a stochastic control tree to your optimization problem' with a k-ary tree branching at interior branching times and ensemble members clustered to paths - precisely the scenario-tree formulation described. EXACTLY 15 example directories: basic, cascading_channels, channel_pulse, channel_wave_damping, ensemble, fallback_option, goal_programming, integrator_delay, lookup_table, mixed_integer, pumped_hydropower_system, simulation, simulation_with_custom_equations, single_reservoir, step_response. single_reservoir.py is EXACTLY 76 lines with VolumeRangeGoal priority=1, MinimizeQpumpGoal priority=2, MinimizeChangeInQpumpGoal priority=3.
confirmed_sources.relevance: Two designs worth stealing without adopting the framework: the goal-programming priority ladder (replaces AquaSync's weighted-sum objective with an explainable priority order a regulator can read) and ControlTreeMixin's scenario tree (one here-and-now release decision across a branching forecast ensemble).
confirmed_sources.content_matches_claim: yes - and unusually precisely. I independently reproduced the 16,410-line and 76-line counts exactly, and confirmed all 15 examples and all three goal priorities.
confirmed_sources.caveat: The Modelica lock-in verdict is CONFIRMED by exhaustive per-example check. All 13 optimisation examples import ModelicaMixin; the only two examples that do not (simulation, simulation_with_custom_equations) are SIMULATION examples and both still ship a .mo file. There is genuinely no Python-only model-definition path on the optimisation side. The 'do not port' verdict stands. Note the goals are expressed over a pump flow (Qpump), not a generic release, in the single_reservoir example.

confirmed_sources.name: Lake Mendocino FIRO Final Viability Assessment (Dec 2020)
confirmed_sources.what_it_provides: Verified by extracting all 297,890 characters of text. PDF /Title metadata: 'Lake Mendocino Forecast Informed Reservoir Operations: Final Viability Assessment'; /Author 'FIRO Steering Committee'; created 2020-12-28. Cover page reads 'December 2020'. Steering Committee co-chaired by Jay Jasperse (Sonoma Water) and F. Martin Ralph (CW3E/Scripps), with USACE, USBR, NOAA/NMFS and CA DWR members. Contains verbatim: 'Lake Mendocino storage increased by 19 percent (more than 11,000 acre-feet) during major deviation operations in WY 2020'; 'WY 2020 was the third driest ... 127-year record'; sections 4.1.1 WY 2019 Major Deviation and WY 2020 Major Deviation; Water Control Manual history 'Original 1959 Updated 1986 Minor revisions 2003'.
confirmed_sources.relevance: The evidence base for arguing FIRO to KSEB/KSDMA: a regulator-grade document showing a conservative federal dam operator accepting forecast-informed operations, with quantified benefit. The HEMP evaluation framework it uses is a reusable template for structuring an AquaSync viability case.
confirmed_sources.content_matches_claim: yes - every numeric claim (19%, >11,000 acre-feet, WY2019/WY2020 deviations, third-driest in 127 years, WCM updated only twice since 1959) was located verbatim in the extracted text.
confirmed_sources.caveat: One timing nuance: 'FIRO is now authorised in the USACE Water Control Manual' overstates what THIS document says. The Dec 2020 FVA recommends a five-year major deviation and a WCM update (section 6.1); as of the FVA itself, FIRO was being delivered through major deviations, not yet through an updated WCM. The '1959 + updated only twice' framing is fully supported (1986 update, 2003 minor revisions).
confirmed_sources.download_hint: direct PDF download, 11,297,686 bytes, no auth

confirmed_sources.name: Prado Dam FIRO Final Viability Assessment (2023)
confirmed_sources.what_it_provides: Verified by extracting all 300,856 characters. Created 2023-11-28. Prado Dam Steering Committee co-chaired by Orange County Water District (Greg Woodside 2017-2023, then Adam Hutchinson 2023-present) and F. Martin Ralph (CW3E). Suggested citation: Ralph, F. M., Hutchinson, A., et al. (2023), 'Prado Dam Forecast Informed Reservoir Operations Final Viability Assessment', UC San Diego. Real verified key findings: FIRO strategies at elevations 508-512 ft yield 4,000-6,000 acre-feet/year of additional groundwater recharge; raising the maximum buffer pool to 520 ft yields about 12,000 ac-ft/year; the Virtual EFO scenario produced ~6,600 acre-feet of additional end-of-April storage; the current buffer pool holds a maximum 20,000 acre-feet at elevation 505 ft.
confirmed_sources.relevance: Second completed FVA and the closest FIRO analogue to a conjunctive-use objective. Useful as a second regulator-grade precedent, with the correct numbers.
confirmed_sources.content_matches_claim: partly - the document is genuine and confirms Prado FIRO viability in 2023, but the headline number attributed to it is fabricated. See caveat.
confirmed_sources.caveat: FABRICATED FIGURE: the string '23,000' appears ZERO times in the entire 300,856-character document. The claim 'up to 23,000 acre-feet of additional recharge in wet years' is not supported by the source cited. The actual reported benefits are 4,000-6,000 ac-ft/yr (508-512 ft), ~12,000 ac-ft/yr (520 ft) and ~6,600 ac-ft (Virtual EFO). Use those numbers. (Minor curiosity: the published PDF's own suggested citation still contains an unfilled placeholder, 'escholarship.org/uc/item/xxxxx'.)
confirmed_sources.download_hint: direct PDF download, 9,969,733 bytes, no auth

confirmed_sources.relevance: The closest published analogue to AquaSync's revenue-side problem (intraday, multi-reservoir, time-varying prices), and the only RL reservoir repo with a genuine Gymnasium env plus MILP and metaheuristic baselines to compare against. Python 3.12, MIT.
confirmed_sources.content_matches_claim: yes - and the claimed paper title matched the DOI exactly. The repo is somewhat richer than described: the source list mentioned 'heuristic baselines' but not that the heuristic is specifically PSO, nor that the RL side is a full Gymnasium + Stable-Baselines3 pipeline.
confirmed_sources.caveat: Default branch is 'master', not 'main'. Datasets, MILP/PSO solution files and RL model weights are all hosted on OneDrive links rather than in the repo. Small project (5 stars); README text is stale in places (still says the RL paper is unpublished though it appeared in Jan 2025).

confirmed_sources.name: cylin928/HydroCNHS
confirmed_sources.what_it_provides: 'A Python Package of Hydrological Model for Coupled Natural-Human Systems'. Verified by cloning: the four agent APIs are all genuinely present - Dam, RiverDiv, Conveying and InSitu. DEAP-based calibration harness confirmed present.
confirmed_sources.relevance: Moderate. The agent-API pattern (a Dam agent embedded in a semi-distributed hydrological model) is a reasonable architectural reference for coupling AquaSync's reservoir operations to its SCS-CN runoff and Muskingum routing, but AquaSync already has a working coupling.
confirmed_sources.content_matches_claim: partly - the four agent APIs and the DEAP calibration harness are confirmed, but the hydrology-options claim is wrong. See caveat.
confirmed_sources.caveat: CORRECTION: HydroCNHS does NOT offer HYMOD. I cloned the repo and grepped case-insensitively across every file - zero occurrences of 'hymod'. Only two rainfall-runoff options exist: GWLF and ABCD. The claimed 'GWLF, ABCD, HYMOD' is a one-third fabrication.

rejected.name: Borg MOEA project site
rejected.reason: URL is live (200) and the prior agent's licensing warning is CORRECT and now double-confirmed - but that is precisely why it must not appear on a list of OPEN-SOURCE sources. borgmoea.org states verbatim: 'Borg is freely available for academic and non-commercial use. Use this site to learn more about the Borg MOEA and request access to its source code' and 'Please complete the Google form below to request access... You will receive an e-mail within three business days'. The Cornell Reed Group page independently repeats the academic/non-commercial restriction. This is not open source, it is gated non-commercial access, and AquaSync is explicitly destined for KSEB - a commercial/government utility. Adopting it would poison the deliverable. Use pymoo (Apache-2.0) instead. Retained above only as context inside the Reed Group index entry.

rejected.name: bernardoct/WaterPaths
rejected.reason: GitHub repo exists (23 stars, Apache-2.0, verified via API) but fails on both relevance and liveness. Last pushed 2022-01-04 - dead for over four and a half years. More importantly it solves a different problem: multi-utility water-supply INVESTMENT portfolios and risk-of-failure infrastructure pathways under deep uncertainty, not reservoir operations. It is also C++ and coupled to Borg, inheriting the licensing trap above. Nothing here transfers to a Periyar operations twin.

rejected.name: FeralFlows/pysedsim
rejected.reason: GitHub repo exists (18 stars, BSD-2-Clause, verified via API) but last pushed 2020-07-22 - dead for six years. Its distinguishing feature is SEDIMENT simulation for dam siting and sediment-management design, which AquaSync does not model at all. Its optimisation path is Borg-coupled. The hydropower component adds nothing AquaSync lacks.

rejected.name: Critical-Infrastructure-Systems-Lab/VICResOpt
rejected.reason: GitHub repo exists (35 stars) and the NSGA-II driver claim is TRUE - I confirmed Routing/OptCalib/autocalieNSGAII.py, multicalieNSGAII.py and optimization.py. Rejected anyway on licensing: the GitHub API reports no licence and I confirmed there is NO LICENSE file in the repo at all. Absent an explicit licence, default copyright applies (all rights reserved) - a harder blocker for a KSEB-bound project than GPL, and the source list never mentioned it. Its companion VICRes has the same problem. Compounding this: dead since 2023-08-08, and using it would require adopting the entire VIC hydrologic model, discarding AquaSync's SCS-CN runoff and its level-storage law already calibrated to r2=0.9957.

rejected.name: pywr/pywr-next (Pywr 2.0, Rust)
rejected.reason: Every fact the prior agent reported is confirmed exactly - 12 stars, 54 open issues, created 2020-11-17, description still verbatim 'An experimental repository exploring ideas for a major revision to Pywr using Rust as a backend', and every GitHub release flagged prerelease=true (v2.0.0-beta1 2025-10-06 through v2.0.0-beta4 2026-07-09). Its own verdict, 'NOT ready - do not build on it', is correct, so it does not belong on a list of sources to adopt. One correction: the '2.0.0b6 pushed to PyPI 2026-08-25' claim is accurate as to version and date (uploaded 2026-08-25T23:27:17) but that artefact ships under the `pywr` PyPI package name, not a `pywr-next` package. Note also pywr-next is MIT-licensed, unlike GPL-3.0 pywr 1.x - relevant if it ever does mature.

verification_notes: FABRICATED NUMBER - Prado FVA. The claim 'up to 23,000 acre-feet of additional recharge in wet years' is NOT in the document cited. I downloaded the PDF and extracted all 300,856 characters; the string '23,000' occurs ZERO times. The document's actual key findings are 4,000-6,000 ac-ft/year additional groundwater recharge at buffer-pool elevations 508-512 ft, about 12,000 ac-ft/year at 520 ft, and ~6,600 ac-ft additional end-of-April storage under the Virtual EFO scenario (the 20,000 ac-ft figure that does appear is the CURRENT buffer pool capacity at elev. 505 ft, not a benefit). This is exactly the failure mode the project brief warned about. Use the real numbers.

MISDESCRIBED FILE - SSJRB perfect_forecast.py. Claimed to be 'an explicit perfect-foresight baseline - exactly AquaSync's current assumption, isolated so the gap can be measured'. It is not. I read the whole 1,883-byte file: it is a data-preparation script that builds a perfect-forecast netCDF by copying observed inflows forward into a (site, time, ensemble, lead) array, then plots and writes it. No reservoir model, no simulation, no gap measurement. The foresight gap is actually measured by swapping the Qf array in train_firo.py / simulate_firo.py. The underlying research idea is sound; the file-level description is wrong.

FACTUAL ERROR - HydroCNHS hydrology options. Claimed 'GWLF, ABCD, HYMOD'. I cloned the repo and grepped case-insensitively across every file: zero occurrences of 'hymod'. Only GWLF and ABCD exist. The four agent APIs (Dam, RiverDiv, Conveying, InSitu) and the DEAP calibration harness are confirmed genuine.

RESEARCH CODE, NOT LIBRARIES - three undisclosed frictions in the FIRO repos that the 'ready to port in 1-2 days' framing glosses over. (1) Robust-FIRO MPCProblem.py line 4 is a bare, unguarded `import mosek` and run() defaults to solver='MOSEK', a COMMERCIAL solver; CLARABEL is a real supported branch (line 84) and does work, but you must pass it explicitly AND still pip install mosek or delete line 4, or the module raises ImportError. (2) SSJRB train_firo.py does not run as committed - line 82 calls DE(opt_wrapper, bounds=bounds, ...) but `bounds` is defined only inside a commented-out block at line 63, so it raises NameError. (3) Neither repo ships its forecast data: Robust-FIRO needs Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15041287, confirmed via DataCite), SSJRB needs a UC Davis Box link (confirmed 200). All three FIRO academic repos have 1 star EACH; Robust-FIRO last pushed 2025-03-18, SSJRB 2024-05-20. Expect no maintenance, no issue response, no API stability. Separately, syn-forecast_stochastic is a MIXED R + Python codebase (R packages future, DEoptim, twosamples, ncdf4), which the source list did not mention.

ALL SELF-REPORTED BENCHMARK TIMINGS ARE UNREPRODUCED. The prior agent reported running things locally: the Idukki-scale MPC port (45 solves in 0.39 s), the rtc-tools single_reservoir example (3.07 s), the grid-vs-NSGA-II head-to-head (2.02 s vs 2.31 s on 4,800 evals), the pywr install (37 packages, 30 s) and the CasADi bundled-plugin enumeration. I checked this environment's Python: casadi, rtctools, pymoca, cvxpy, pywr and pymoo are ALL absent, so none of it could be re-run. This is not evidence the claims are false - the documentary claims I could check were unusually accurate (16,410 lines, 76 lines, 194 lines, 88 releases and every dependency specifier matched exactly), which lends real credibility. But treat the timings and the CasADi solver list as unverified, and re-run them before relying on the 'install burden is low' conclusion.

RL NEGATIVE FINDING SURVIVES, with two corrections. I re-ran six GitHub searches adversarially. 'reservoir+operation+DDPG' does return 0 repositories, exactly as claimed. But broader searches surface things the prior agent missed. The top hit by stars for 'reservoir + reinforcement learning' is Muzhaffar99/RL-Based-Control-of-Reservoir-Systems-Using-SAC-and-PPO at 38 stars - I checked it and it is MATLAB/Simulink water-TANK level control (single-tank and quadruple-tank PID benchmarks, an MSc dissertation in automatic control), not reservoir operations, so it correctly does not count. Most other high-star hits are reservoir COMPUTING (echo state networks) or PETROLEUM reservoirs (EclGym, DRL_CLRM). One genuine miss: Sarmadzandi/Deep-Multi-Agent-Reinforcement-Learning-Reservoir-Operations (4 stars, MIT, 2024-08) is real reservoir-operations MARL. Second correction: 'there is no reservoir-RL equivalent of stable-baselines3' is fair, but flowing-basin does ship a working Gymnasium environment trained with Stable-Baselines3, so 'NO usable open code' is slightly too strong. The practical conclusion - RL is not a credible route for AquaSync now - stands.

LICENCE CORRECTIONS the GitHub API gets wrong, all of which matter for a KSEB-bound deliverable. MOEAFramework reports NOASSERTION only because its licence sits in a file named COPYING; I read it and it is LGPL-3.0-or-later. SDDP.jl also reports NOASSERTION; its LICENSE.md states plainly 'SDDP.jl is licensed under the Mozilla Public License, Version 2.0' - permissive and safe to build on. Conversely, two repos have NO licence file at all (VICResOpt and its companion VICRes), which means all-rights-reserved by default - a harder blocker than GPL, and never mentioned in the source list.

OVERSTATED BY DEGREE, not fabricated. (a) Lake Mendocino: 'FIRO is now authorised in the USACE Water Control Manual' overstates what the Dec 2020 FVA itself says - that document RECOMMENDS a five-year major deviation and a WCM update; at the time of writing FIRO ran through major deviations. The '1959, updated only twice' framing IS supported (the PDF gives 'Original 1959, Updated 1986, Minor revisions 2003'), and the 19% / >11,000 acre-feet / third-driest-in-127-years figures are all verbatim correct. (b) Water Programming blog: 'HydroCNHS walkthroughs' is generous - archive search returns about one such post, though Borg, MOEA diagnostics and many-objective reservoir coverage is genuinely substantial. (c) Pywr's [opt] extra pulls pygmo as well as platypus-opt.

UNVERIFIABLE, PLUS BOT-BLOCKED ITEMS CONFIRMED BY OTHER MEANS. HEC-ResSim 'v4.1, April 2026' could NOT be checked - both hec.usace.army.mil URLs returned status 000 (connection failure; the .mil host is unreachable from here, not merely bot-blocked). The surrounding argument is consistent with what is known about HEC-ResSim, but drop the version specificity. Per the brief's instruction on bot-blocked hosts: zenodo.org returns 403 ('Access to this resource has been restricted due to unusual traffic from your network') so the Robust-FIRO data DOI was confirmed instead via the DataCite API as 'wltaylor/Robust-FIRO: Initial Release' (2025); doi.org redirects to MDPI and INFORMS both returned 403 to curl, so DOI 10.3390/math13010151 and DOI 10.1287/ijoc.2020.0987 were confirmed via the Crossref API. Two repos use a 'master' default branch, so raw.githubusercontent paths built on 'main' 404: iRONS and flowing-basin.

WHAT HELD UP BEST, for calibration of how much to trust the rest. The two verdicts I tried hardest to break both survived. (1) RTC-Tools' Modelica lock-in: I scripted a per-example check across all 15 examples - every one of the 13 optimisation examples imports ModelicaMixin, and the only two that do not are simulation examples that still ship a .mo file. 'Do not port, steal the two designs' is correct. (2) Borg's licensing trap: confirmed verbatim from two independent pages. Beyond that, the precision of the checkable claims was striking - 16,410 src lines, 76-line single_reservoir.py with goals at priority 1/2/3, 194-line MPCProblem.py with the exact stated objective, 15 examples, 88 PyPI releases, every rtc-tools/pymoo/DEAP dependency specifier, iRONS file sizes to the byte, all seven M3O method directories, and all eleven Reed Group index entries. The errors cluster in one place: claims about documents and features the agent described but did not actually open - the Prado figure, the SSJRB file, and HYMOD.
